stem: A postpartum client has heavier-than-expected vaginal bleeding. Which assessment finding most strongly supports uterine atony as the source of the hemorrhage?

options.A: A soft, boggy, enlarged uterus with ongoing bleeding.
options.B: A firm, well-contracted uterus with persistent bright vaginal bleeding.
options.C: A firm uterus with a tender expanding vulvar mass and increasing pelvic pressure.
options.D: Diffuse oozing from venipuncture sites despite a well-contracted uterus.

rationale: A is correct. Uterine atony is inadequate uterine contraction and commonly presents with a soft, boggy or noncontracted enlarged uterus accompanied by excessive postpartum bleeding. B is more concerning for genital tract trauma when bleeding persists despite a firm uterus. C is more consistent with a genital tract hematoma rather than uterine atony. D suggests a coagulation disorder such as disseminated intravascular coagulation. Because postpartum hemorrhage can have more than one cause, rapid assessment of uterine tone, the genital tract, placental completeness, and coagulation findings should occur while treatment and resuscitation proceed.
educational_objective: Differentiate uterine atony from other postpartum hemorrhage causes by recognizing the characteristic soft, boggy, enlarged uterus and by contrasting it with trauma- or coagulopathy-related bleeding despite adequate uterine tone.
source_organization: National Library of Medicine / NCBI StatPearls
source_version_date: Current StatPearls 2026 edition pages accessed 2026-08-17; Uterine Atony chapter last updated July 4, 2023
source_locator: Postpartum Hemorrhage — History and Physical / Clinical Evaluation: evaluate the cause rapidly; a soft, boggy or noncontracted uterus is the common finding with uterine atony; genital tract lacerations and hematomas should be assessed; widespread bleeding including from venipuncture sites indicates DIC. Uterine Atony — History and Physical/Evaluation: bimanual or direct examination reveals a boggy, soft, unusually enlarged uterus, typically with coexistent bleeding; diagnosis is prompted by excessive blood loss with a flaccid enlarged uterus.
source_claim_supported: A soft or boggy enlarged uterus with excessive postpartum bleeding strongly supports uterine atony, whereas persistent bleeding with a firm uterus should prompt assessment for trauma, hematoma, retained tissue, or coagulopathy depending on associated findings.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Physiological Adaptation, page 14: recognize signs and symptoms of client complications and intervene. Appendix A, Physiological Adaptation — Alterations in Body Systems, page 47: provide care for client experiencing complications of pregnancy/labor/delivery including hemorrhage; Medical Emergencies, page 48.
blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — postpartum hemorrhage and uterine atony recognition
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source item from a generic hemorrhage-recognition question into a cause-identification assessment. The final distractors represent realistic alternative postpartum hemorrhage etiologies rather than normal/no-action statements and avoid unsupported numeric blood-loss thresholds.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.clinical_category: postpartum hemorrhage / uterine atony / hemorrhage-source assessment
audit_findings.source_audit: Verified against current NCBI Postpartum Hemorrhage and Uterine Atony chapters. The core finding of a soft/boggy noncontracted uterus is explicit; the same source differentiates laceration, hematoma, retained tissue and DIC during rapid etiologic assessment.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: A directly matches uterine atony findings. B preserves a plausible trauma pattern with a firm uterus. C pairs a firm uterus with an expanding hematoma pattern. D uses the source-supported clue of diffuse venipuncture-site bleeding for coagulopathy. The rationale does not assign a single cause solely from blood volume or vital-sign thresholds.
audit_findings.choice_A: Correct; boggy enlarged uterus with ongoing postpartum bleeding is the strongest atony pattern.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect but plausible; persistent bleeding despite adequate uterine tone points away from atony and toward genital tract trauma.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect but plausible; a tender expanding vulvar mass and pressure suggest hematoma.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect but plausible; diffuse oozing with a contracted uterus suggests a coagulation disorder rather than isolated atony.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Multiple causes of postpartum hemorrhage can coexist, so the stem asks which finding most strongly supports atony. Only A contains the defining uterine-tone abnormality.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are postpartum assessment patterns with comparable detail and each represents a clinically relevant hemorrhage mechanism.
audit_findings.blueprint: The item directly tests recognition of postpartum hemorrhage etiology and rapid complication assessment under Physiological Adaptation.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Rechecked whether a firm fundus can coexist with focal lower-segment atony and whether mixed etiologies can occur. Because those exceptions exist, the item uses 'most strongly supports' rather than an absolute diagnostic statement. The alternatives remain defensible competing mechanisms but not equally correct. No unsupported threshold or second answer remained.
